content: The document outlines detailed strategies and activities for strengthening immunization systems, improving vaccine coverage, and ensuring financial sustainability in line with the WHO-UNICEF guidelines for comprehensive Multi-Year Plans (cMYP) for immunization. 1. Surveillance and Reporting: Active surveillance for Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) should be strengthened in all districts to ensure early detection and response. A centralized database for integrated disease surveillance should be established to streamline data collection and analysis. Active case-based surveillance for measles and rubella should be implemented as part of the integrated vaccine-preventable disease surveillance system. Monthly meetings for surveillance focal points should be conducted to review progress and address challenges. District-level emergency preparedness and prevention plans should be developed to respond effectively to outbreaks. Data analysis and utilization at all levels should be enhanced to inform decision-making and improve program outcomes. 2. Capacity Building for Adverse Events Following Immunization (AEFI): New district-level vaccine-preventable disease (VPD) focal points should be trained in AEFI management to ensure timely and effective responses. Cold-chain systems and logistics should be assessed, and additional equipment should be procured to support the introduction of new vaccines, such as the rotavirus vaccine. Regular supply of auto-disable (AD) syringes to all districts and health centers should be ensured, and policies for their use across all vaccines should be implemented. 3. Program Management: Technical Interagency Coordinating Committee (ICC) meetings should be held monthly to review program performance and address operational issues. Districts and health facilities should be supervised regularly to ensure adherence to immunization protocols. Health workers should be trained in Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI) management to enhance their skills and knowledge. Implementation of Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) should be supported through routine vaccination activities. Staff retention and motivation in primary healthcare (PHC) should be improved through performance-based management systems and orientation programs for new staff. 4. Legislation and Policy: Immunization financing should be supported by legislation that establishes a dedicated budget line for vaccines in the national health budget. National immunization policies should be updated regularly, with input from the National Immunization Technical Advisory Group (NITAG) and other stakeholders. Advocacy efforts should include presentations to parliament on immunization performance to secure political and financial support. 5. Cold-Chain and Logistics: Districts should maintain adequate numbers of functional cold-chain equipment to ensure vaccine potency. Regular inventory assessments of cold-chain, transport, and waste management equipment should be conducted. Waste management plans should be developed and implemented to ensure safe disposal of immunization-related waste. 6. Immunization Services: Routine immunization coverage targets should be progressively increased, with a goal of achieving 95% DTP3 coverage by 2018. Equity in immunization coverage should be addressed by reducing the gap between the lowest and highest socio-economic quintiles. Drop-out rates between DTP1 and DTP3 should be minimized, with a target of less than 5% by 2018. High-risk communities should be identified, and efforts should be made to ensure all households are registered for health services. 7. Financial Sustainability: National expenditures on immunization-specific operating and capital costs should be monitored as a share of GDP, adjusted for debt service, to assess financial self-sufficiency. A comprehensive financial plan should be developed, including a five-year budget, identified financing sources, and commitments from development partners. Efficient use of resources should be ensured by purchasing quality vaccines through global procurement mechanisms and minimizing wastage. 8. Monitoring and Evaluation: Annual and quarterly planning reviews should be conducted at all levels of the health system to assess progress and address gaps. A national database of district-level indicators should be established to track immunization performance. Micro-planning workshops should be conducted in all districts to improve service delivery and coverage. 9. New Vaccine Introduction: The introduction of new vaccines, such as pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV), should be supported by achieving high coverage rates and ensuring adequate cold-chain capacity. 10. Injection Safety: All districts should be supplied with sufficient numbers of AD syringes for routine immunizations to ensure safe injection practices. 11. Stakeholder Engagement: Regular consultations with ministries, parliament, and civil society organizations (CSOs) should be conducted to disseminate information on immunization impacts and financing gaps. The ICC should include representatives from CSOs, academia, and the private sector to broaden stakeholder participation. 12. Community Engagement: High-risk communities should be engaged through collaboration with local authorities to ensure comprehensive registration and access to health services. These strategies and activities are designed to strengthen immunization systems, improve vaccine coverage, and ensure the financial sustainability of immunization programs, ultimately contributing to better health outcomes.
